narration.text: This section summarizes Alabama's graduated driver license rules, the staged system that gives young drivers experience before full privileges. The summary names the graduated license law, with amendments that took effect in two thousand ten. In this lesson you will learn who the rules do not apply to, including drivers eighteen or older, some seventeen-year-olds, married or head-of-household teens and those relieved of minority status, and which drivers the restrictions do apply to. Knowing whether the rules cover you is the first step.

Alabama's graduated driver license rules do not apply to anyone eighteen years of age or older. They also do not apply to a seventeen-year-old or older driver who has held a valid license for six months or more. A person sixteen or older who is married or is the head of a household is exempt from the graduated rules. Someone who has been legally relieved of minority status is also outside the graduated rules. So age, time licensed and legal status can each take a young driver out of the graduated system. Check both age and time licensed. The restrictions apply at sixteen.

lines.text: Seventeen and licensed under six months.

narration.text: The license restrictions apply to drivers who are sixteen, and to seventeen-year-olds who have held a license for less than six months. Those are the drivers who must follow the passenger, late-night and handheld-device limits you will learn in a later lesson. So a seventeen-year-old who got a license only a few months ago is still restricted, while one who has held a license for six months or more is not. Counting how long you have held your license is just as important as knowing your age. Check both age and time licensed. The restrictions apply at sixteen.

Here is the trap. The two age-based exemptions work differently. Anyone eighteen or older is exempt outright, with no other condition. A seventeen-year-old is free of the graduated rules only after holding a valid license for six months. So a seventeen-year-old with a brand-new license is still covered, but an eighteen-year-old with a brand-new license is not. When a question gives you a driver's age, check whether it also gives how long the license has been held, because at seventeen that detail decides the answer. Check both age and time licensed.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old is married. Do the graduated rules apply? Decide on your answer first. The answer is no. A person sixteen or older who is married or is the head of a household is exempt from the graduated rules. Other exemptions cover anyone eighteen or older, seventeen-year-olds who have held a valid license six months or more, and anyone legally relieved of minority status. Every other sixteen-year-old, and seventeen-year-olds licensed under six months, must follow the restrictions. Check both age and time licensed.

To sum up, the graduated license rules do not apply to anyone eighteen or older, to a seventeen-year-old or older driver licensed for six months or more, to a sixteen-year-old or older who is married or head of a household, or to someone relieved of minority status. The restrictions apply to sixteen-year-olds and to seventeen-year-olds who have held a license for less than six months. The summary names the law with amendments that took effect in two thousand ten. Next you will see the path from a learner license to an unrestricted one. Check both age and time licensed.

narration.text: This lesson follows a young driver's path from a learner license toward an unrestricted license. You will learn the requirements a driver under eighteen must meet before applying for an unrestricted license, who may supervise a fifteen-year-old learner, the role of a driving instructor, and the parental permission a sixteen-year-old needs. These rules make sure young drivers build experience with an approved adult beside them before driving on their own. Pay attention to the ages and to the six-month period, because those details decide what a learner may do.

lines.text: Six months on a learner license.

narration.text: A person under eighteen cannot apply for an unrestricted license until holding a learner license for at least six months with no restriction violations, and must be seventeen. So there are three conditions together: six months, a clean record on the restrictions, and age seventeen. Missing any one of them means waiting longer. A sixteen-year-old needs a parent's or legal guardian's permission both to get a license and to drive without supervision, which keeps parents involved in the decision about when a teen is ready. Supervisors sit in the front seat.

A fifteen-year-old holding a valid learner license may drive only when a parent, legal guardian, licensed driver aged twenty-one or older, or licensed or certified driving instructor occupies the front seat beside the driver. Each approved supervisor must occupy the front seat beside the learner. So the supervisor must be on that approved list and must sit in the front seat. A friend or relative under twenty-one does not qualify, unless they are a parent or guardian, and someone in the back seat does not count as supervision. Supervisors sit in the front seat.

lines.text: For a license and solo driving.

narration.text: A sixteen-year-old needs a parent's or legal guardian's permission both to get a license and to drive without supervision. That permission is a separate requirement from passing the tests. Combined with the other rules, it means parents play a key role at each stage: supervising or approving supervisors while the teen is fifteen, giving permission at sixteen, and later consenting to certain late-night trips. A teen who wants more independence needs both the legal requirements and a parent's or guardian's approval. Supervisors sit in the front seat.

Here is the trap. Two different rules involve who rides with a young driver. A fifteen-year-old learner's supervisor must be a parent, a legal guardian, a licensed driver at least twenty-one, or a licensed or certified driving instructor occupying the front seat beside the driver. Separately, a restricted driver may carry only one nonfamily passenger besides the parent, guardian, or supervising licensed driver at least twenty-one. So the supervisor rule is about who must be beside a learner, and the passenger rule is about how many friends a restricted driver may bring. Do not mix the two when answering questions. Supervisors sit in the front seat.

Here is a quick check: can a licensed driving instructor serve as the supervisor for a fifteen-year-old learner? Decide on your answer first. The answer is yes, when the instructor sits in the front seat beside the learner. A licensed or certified driving instructor satisfies the supervision rule, just as a parent, a legal guardian, or a licensed driver twenty-one or older seated beside the learner does. A licensed friend younger than twenty-one, or anyone riding in the back seat, would not meet the rule. Supervisors sit in the front seat.

lines.text: Six clean months and age seventeen.

narration.text: To wrap up, a fifteen-year-old with a learner license may drive only with a parent, a legal guardian, a licensed driver twenty-one or older, or a licensed or certified driving instructor seated beside them. A sixteen-year-old needs a parent's or guardian's permission to get a license and to drive without supervision. A driver under eighteen cannot apply for an unrestricted license until holding a learner license for at least six months with no restriction violations and reaching seventeen. Supervisor rules are separate from the passenger limit for restricted drivers.

why_how.text: Restricted drivers face limits on passengers, late-night driving and handheld devices to reduce risk while they gain experience.
Knowing the exceptions lets restricted drivers handle work, school and emergencies.

scenario.text: Riley, sixteen, wants to drive home from a regular work shift that ends at one in the morning.

reasoning.text: A restricted driver may not drive between midnight and six unless an exception applies, and going to or from a regular workplace is an exception.

result.text: Riley may drive home from work, but not to a friend's house afterward.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a restricted driver may carry several friends if they all are licensed.

correction.text: A restricted driver may carry no more than one nonfamily passenger besides the parent, guardian or supervising adult driver.

memory_support.text: One friend, no phone, home by midnight.

answer.text: No, driving while using any handheld communication device is barred.

rationale.text: The restrictions bar handheld devices, and breaking that rule extends the restricted period or suspends the license.

narration.text: This lesson covers the three limits on restricted drivers: how many nonfamily passengers they may carry, when they may not drive at night, and the ban on handheld communication devices. You will also learn the exceptions to the late-night limit, such as trips to work, school-sponsored events and religious-sponsored events, and the emergency exception. These limits target the situations where new drivers face the most risk: distraction from friends in the car, driving late at night, and taking eyes off the road for a phone. One nonfamily passenger at most.

A restricted driver may carry no more than one nonfamily passenger besides the parent, guardian or supervising licensed driver aged at least twenty-one, a limit cut from four in two thousand ten. The restrictions also bar driving while using any handheld communication device, and violating that rule extends the graduated period and or suspends the license. So a restricted driver keeps the car mostly free of distractions: at most one friend along, and no phone in hand while driving. Family members do not count toward the one-passenger limit.

lines.text: Unless a parent is along or an exception.

narration.text: A restricted young driver may not operate a vehicle from midnight to six a.m. unless accompanied by a parent or legal guardian, riding with a licensed driver twenty-one or older with parental consent, traveling to or from regular work or a school- or religious-sponsored event, or driving for a medical, fire, or law-enforcement emergency. Every exception requires meeting the exact condition listed in the summary. Outside those exceptions, a restricted driver stays off the road from midnight until six. One nonfamily passenger at most.

Here is the trap. Driving between twelve midnight and six a.m. is allowed with a parent or guardian, while riding with another adult licensee twenty-one or older also needs parental consent. So a restricted driver cannot simply bring along any adult and drive at two in the morning. The other adult must be a licensee at least twenty-one, and the parents must consent. Other exceptions cover trips to work, school-sponsored events, religious-sponsored events, and real medical, fire or law enforcement emergencies. One nonfamily passenger at most.

Here is a quick check: a restricted driver wants to hold a phone to check directions while driving. Is that allowed? Decide on your answer first. The answer is no. The restrictions bar driving while using any handheld communication device, and violating that rule extends the graduated period and or suspends the license. Pull over safely first if you need to check directions. The other two limits still apply too: no more than one nonfamily passenger, and no driving between midnight and six a.m. unless an exception applies. One nonfamily passenger at most.

lines.text: Midnight to six off the road.

narration.text: To close, a restricted driver may carry no more than one nonfamily passenger besides the parent, guardian or supervising adult, a limit cut from four in two thousand ten. A restricted driver may not drive between midnight and six a.m. unless a parent or guardian is along or an exception applies: an adult licensee twenty-one or older with parental consent, a medical, fire or law enforcement emergency, or trips to or from a regular workplace, a school-sponsored event or a religious-sponsored event. Handheld communication devices are barred while driving.

Some violations extend the restricted period, while serious offenses bring a suspension.

result.text: Casey can be cited for the passenger violation too, which brings no points but extends the restricted period by six months or until eighteen.

correction.text: They add no points and no criminal penalty, but they extend the restricted period by six months or until the driver turns eighteen.

prompt.text: What kind of offense is breaking a graduated license condition?

answer.text: A traffic violation, with no criminal penalty or court costs.

rationale.text: Breaking a condition is a traffic violation but carries no criminal penalty or court costs.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens when a restricted driver breaks the graduated license rules or commits other offenses. You will learn what kind of offense a restriction violation is, when an officer may issue a citation for one, whether points are added, how the restricted period is extended, and which convictions bring an automatic sixty-day suspension. The key idea is that there are two levels: restriction violations extend the time you stay restricted, while serious driving offenses take your license away for a time. Restriction slips extend; serious offenses suspend.

Breaking a graduated-license condition is a traffic violation but carries no criminal penalty or court costs. A citation for a graduated-license violation is issued only when the driver is stopped and cited for a separate violation of the law. No points go on the record for violating the graduated-license restrictions. So an officer cannot stop a teen just to check the passenger count or the time of night, but if the teen is stopped and cited for something else, such as speeding, the restriction violation can be cited too. Restriction slips extend; serious offenses suspend.

lines.text: Violation: extend six months or to eighteen.

narration.text: Any restriction violation extends the restricted period by six months or until the driver turns eighteen. A restricted driver's license is automatically suspended for sixty days after a second moving violation conviction or any conviction worth four or more points. The same sixty-day suspension follows a conviction for failing to give information or render aid, racing, fleeing or eluding an officer, reckless driving, illegal passing or driving on the wrong side. So small slips keep you restricted longer, and serious offenses take the license for sixty days.

title.text: No points is not no penalty

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because restriction violations add no points and bring no criminal penalty, some teens think they do not matter. They still extend the restricted period by six months or until the driver turns eighteen. And a GDL citation is never written on its own; the officer must first stop and cite the driver for a separate violation. So the consequences are real, just different from points. A teen who breaks the passenger or curfew limit stays under the restrictions longer, which delays the freedom of an unrestricted license. Restriction slips extend; serious offenses suspend.

Breaking a restriction extends the graduated period, but a second moving violation or a four-point offense brings an automatic sixty-day suspension. The listed serious offenses, including failing to give information or render aid, racing, fleeing or eluding an officer, reckless driving, illegal passing and driving on the wrong side, bring the same sixty-day suspension. Keeping these two levels apart helps you answer questions correctly: a passenger or curfew violation leads to an extension, while a serious moving violation leads to losing the license for sixty days.

narration.text: To finish the section, breaking a graduated license condition is a traffic violation with no criminal penalty, no court costs and no points, and it is cited only along with a separate violation. Any restriction violation still extends the restricted period by six months or until eighteen. A second moving violation conviction, any four-point conviction, or a conviction for failing to give information or render aid, racing, fleeing, reckless driving, illegal passing or driving on the wrong side brings an automatic sixty-day suspension of a restricted driver's license.
